feature shared by the recent wave of HANK models, and which differentiates them from
the baseline New Keynesian model, is the assumption of idiosyncratic shocks to
households’ labor productivity and, hence, to their wage. Those shocks are often
assumed to follow a stochastic process that is consistent with some features of the micro
data. Secondly, it is generally assumed that only a small number of assets can be traded,
and that some exogenous borrowing limit exists. As a result, households cannot
perfectly insure themselves against idiosyncratic risk. Furthermore, a (time-varying)
fraction of households face a binding borrowing constraint, which makes their
consumption respond strongly to fluctuations in current income. The previous features
imply that there is no simple dynamic IS equation like the one described earlier that can
be derived. However, the other two main elements of the basic New Keynesian
framework —the New Keynesian Phillips curve and the interest rate rule—are not
directly affected by the introduction of heterogeneity.
One of the main lessons emerging from the analysis of heterogenous agent New
Keynesian models can be summarized as follows: The presence of uninsurable
idiosyncratic shocks, combined with the existence of borrowing limits, implies that
different households, even if they otherwise appear identical before the shocks arise,
may have at any point in time very different marginal propensities to consume. As a
result, the macroeconomic effects of any aggregate shock will be amplified or
dampened depending on the way the shock (and the changes that it triggers) affects the
distribution of income and wealth across households.
Several recent papers provide an insightful analysis of that mechanism. Auclert (2017)
studies the different channels through which heterogeneity shapes the effect of an
exogenous monetary policy shock on individual and aggregate consumption. Two of
those channels are already present in the representative agent New Keynesian model
(henceforth, RANK, for short): i) intertemporal substitution, in response to changes in
real interest rates; and ii) the change in consumption induced by the resulting changes in
aggregate income, which is a source of a multiplier effect. A HANK economy, on the
other hand, provides three additional channels that occur as a consequence of the
redistribution that takes place in response to a monetary policy change: i) the earnings
heterogeneity channel is associated with the fact that some households see their income
increase more than proportionally to aggregate income, while others lose in relative
terms; ii) the Fisher channel refer to the fact that different households have at any point
in time different net positions in nominal assets, whose real value will be affected by the
change in the price level resulting from the monetary policy intervention; and iii) the
unhedged interest rate exposure channel arises because of likely differences across
households in the mismatch between durations of assets and liabilities (including
planned consumption among the latter).

**Thread Title:** How Our Guild Adapted to the Rise of UniCoin in Cross-Server Trade  

---

**User: PixelNomad**  
So, over the past year, our MMO switched its auction house and player-to-player trades to use UniCoin — the new universal cryptocurrency that works across all servers and regions. At first, I thought it was just a convenience thing, but it’s actually changed the way we interact with players from other countries, and even how our guild handles resources.  

Before UniCoin, each server had its own “gold” or “credits” economy. Prices were wildly different depending on local farming habits, bot activity, or just player culture. If you hopped servers, you’d have to mentally convert values and figure out whether you were getting ripped off. Now, with UniCoin, a rare mount from the Korean server costs the same amount in the European one, at least in nominal terms.  

But what’s fascinating is how the *culture* around trade has shifted. Players are more open to cross-border deals because there’s no need to fuss over exchange rates. Our guild has started doing joint raids with a Brazilian group because we can split loot sales in UniCoin without worrying about mismatched values.  

---

**User: TradeWinds**  
I’ve noticed the same thing in my crafting circles. I make enchanted gear, and before UniCoin, selling to players overseas was a nightmare — you’d have to find a trusted middleman or use third-party sites. Now, I can list my wares in the global marketplace and get buyers from anywhere.  

What’s interesting is that people’s perception of “expensive” items has normalized. In the past, a sword that cost 100k credits on my server might be 5k on another. Players would argue endlessly about which economy was “inflated.” With UniCoin, there’s more consensus about value, though regional scarcity still affects demand. For example, certain crafting materials are abundant in Southeast Asia servers because of local farming meta, so their UniCoin price is lower globally.  

---

**User: LoreKeeper**  
Cultural impact goes beyond just pricing. I’ve found that the shared currency has made players more curious about other regions’ playstyles. When you’re trading directly with someone in another country, you start chatting about their server events, how they farm, what guild politics are like.  

It’s also changed gifting culture. UniCoin transfers are instant and universal, so people send small amounts as “thank-you” for advice or as welcome gifts to new players. It’s created a kind of global player etiquette. I’ve even received UniCoin tips for streaming, from viewers who don’t speak my language but still want to support me.  

---

**User: ByteSmith**  
One thing I’ve been tracking is how the in-game economies have *converged*. With UniCoin, price discrepancies get arbitraged faster. If a rare pet is cheap in one region, traders buy it up and resell it globally. This pushes prices toward a global average.  

That’s great for fairness, but it also means local bargains vanish quickly. Some players miss the thrill of finding a “steal” on their home server. On the flip side, it’s made income from farming or crafting more predictable — you know roughly how much UniCoin you’ll get for your work, no matter where your buyer is.  

---

**User: CrossServerChef**  
From a social standpoint, UniCoin has made cross-cultural guilds more viable. I run a cooking-themed guild that trades in-game food buffs. Before, we had to keep separate ledgers for members in different regions. Now, we pool everything in UniCoin and vote on how to spend it — like funding large-scale feasts during events.  

It’s also reduced misunderstandings. When everyone uses the same currency, there’s less suspicion about whether someone is overcharging due to “foreign prices.” This has built trust, which is huge in collaborative play.  

---

**User: PixelNomad**  
Yeah, trust is a big part of it. The universal currency hasn’t erased all cultural differences — some regions still haggle more, others stick to listed prices — but it’s given us a common ground. I think that’s why cross-server friendships have become more common.  

It’s weird to think that a single fictional coin could have such a big impact on how we play and interact. For me, UniCoin isn’t just about trade; it’s about feeling like we’re part of one big, connected world.

**First-Mover Advantage**  

**Overview**  
First-mover advantage is an economic and strategic concept describing the benefits that accrue to a firm or organization that is the first to enter a particular market or industry segment. By being early to market, the first mover can establish brand recognition, secure strategic resources, build customer loyalty, and shape consumer preferences before competitors arrive. These advantages can translate into sustained profitability and long-term dominance, although they are not guaranteed and depend on the ability of the first mover to maintain its lead over time.  

**Key Characteristics**  
A first mover is typically defined as the earliest entrant into a new product category, technology niche, or geographic market. The advantages associated with this position often include:  

1. **Brand Recognition and Customer Loyalty** – Early entrants have the opportunity to embed their brand in the minds of consumers before alternatives are available. This can lead to strong loyalty that persists even when competitors introduce similar products.  

2. **Control of Key Resources** – In many industries, scarce resources such as prime retail locations, patents, supplier relationships, or distribution channels can be secured by the first company to act. Later entrants must compete for what remains, often at higher cost.  

3. **Technological Leadership** – First movers can set technical standards, influence regulatory frameworks, and define product specifications that competitors may be forced to adopt.  

4. **Economies of Scale** – By establishing production and distribution early, first movers can achieve cost efficiencies sooner than competitors, reinforcing their market position.  

**Historical Examples**  
In the technology sector, companies such as Intel in microprocessors and Amazon in online retail have leveraged early market entry to become industry leaders. Intel’s early dominance in microprocessor design allowed it to dictate industry standards and secure long-term contracts with major computer manufacturers. Amazon, by entering e-commerce before most traditional retailers, built extensive fulfillment networks and customer trust that later entrants struggled to match.  

In retail, Walmart’s early and aggressive expansion into rural and suburban markets in the United States provided it with a vast network of stores and distribution centers ahead of competitors. This physical footprint, combined with advanced supply chain management, allowed Walmart to maintain price leadership and market share for decades.  

In manufacturing, Ford Motor Company’s introduction of the Model T in 1908, along with the adoption of assembly line production, positioned Ford as the dominant automaker in the early 20th century. The company’s innovations in design and manufacturing efficiency created a cost advantage that competitors could not immediately replicate.  

**Sustainability of Advantage**  
While first-mover advantage can be significant, it is not inherently permanent. Competitors may learn from the first mover’s successes and mistakes, entering the market with improved products, lower prices, or more efficient operations. This phenomenon is sometimes referred to as the “fast follower” strategy, where later entrants benefit from the groundwork laid by the first mover without incurring the same initial costs or risks.  

Maintaining a first-mover advantage requires continuous innovation, investment in customer relationships, and adaptation to changing market conditions. Firms that fail to evolve may find their early lead eroded by more agile competitors.  

**Risks and Limitations**  
First movers face substantial uncertainty, as they must invest in product development, market education, and infrastructure without assurance of consumer acceptance. They may encounter unforeseen technical challenges, regulatory hurdles, or shifts in consumer preferences. Additionally, the costs of pioneering a market—research and development, marketing to create demand, and building supply chains—can be high and may not be recoverable if competitors quickly match or surpass the offering.  

**Conclusion**  
First-mover advantage remains a central concept in competitive strategy and economic analysis. Its potential to deliver long-term market leadership has been demonstrated across technology, retail, and manufacturing sectors. However, sustaining this advantage requires strategic foresight and ongoing investment, as the same pioneering qualities that open a market can also invite intense competition from followers seeking to capitalize on the groundwork already laid.

**Finding the Right Price for Vintage Weather Observation Instruments**  

For many collectors, the allure of vintage weather observation instruments lies in their ability to capture a moment in time—both scientifically and aesthetically. Whether it’s a brass aneroid barometer from the early 20th century, a hand‑blown glass storm glass from the Victorian era, or a mid‑century mechanical hygrometer, each piece tells a story about human curiosity and the evolving technology of meteorology. But while acquiring these treasures can be deeply rewarding, determining the ideal price point for a purchase requires a careful balance of research, intuition, and market awareness.

---

### Understanding Rarity

Rarity is often the first factor that comes to mind when assessing value. In the world of vintage weather instruments, rarity can be defined by several variables: limited production runs, the survival rate of the item, and unique design features. A barometer made by a renowned instrument maker who produced only a handful of prototypes will naturally command a higher price than a mass‑market model from the same period. Similarly, instruments that have unusual scales, custom engravings, or mechanisms no longer in production often carry a premium.  

To assess rarity, collectors should consult auction records, specialized dealer catalogs, and museum collections. If an item appears only sporadically in these sources, it may be considered rare enough to justify a higher purchase price.

---

### Historical Significance

Beyond scarcity, historical context profoundly influences value. Instruments tied to notable events, expeditions, or technological breakthroughs can be especially desirable. For example, a barograph used aboard a research vessel during a famous Arctic expedition may be worth significantly more than a similar model with no documented provenance.  

Provenance, when clearly documented, adds credibility and increases desirability among collectors. Original receipts, maker’s markings, and archival photographs serve as tangible proof of an item’s place in history. In such cases, the price point should reflect not only the instrument’s physical attributes but also the intangible prestige that comes with owning a piece of meteorological heritage.

---

### Condition and Functionality

Condition is a universal determinant of value in collectibles, and weather instruments are no exception. A pristine instrument with its original finish, intact glass, and functioning mechanism will generally command a higher price than one with corrosion, missing parts, or non‑working components.  

However, collectors must weigh the importance of functionality against their own goals. Some may prioritize aesthetic condition over operational readiness, especially if the piece will be displayed rather than used. In certain cases, a rare but non‑functional instrument may still merit a high price if restoration is possible without compromising authenticity.

---

### Comparing Market Prices

A practical step in setting a purchase budget is to compare current market prices for similar instruments. This involves reviewing recent auction results, online marketplace listings, and dealer inventories. It’s important to note that prices can vary significantly depending on geographic location, the reputation of the seller, and the venue of sale.  

Collectors should be cautious of anomalies—an unusually low price may indicate undisclosed damage or missing parts, while an unusually high price might reflect a seller’s personal attachment rather than market reality. By identifying a range of typical prices for comparable items, a buyer can determine a fair offer that balances value and affordability.

---

### Factoring Personal Value

While rarity, historical significance, and condition all contribute to market value, personal value is often the deciding factor in a collector’s final price ceiling. An instrument that resonates with one’s own experiences—perhaps a weather vane similar to one seen in childhood, or a rain gauge identical to those used in a local observatory—may justify paying more than the average market rate.  

This subjective element should not be underestimated. A collector’s enjoyment and connection to the piece can make the investment worthwhile, even if the financial appraisal is more modest.

---

### Negotiation and Timing

Finally, timing can influence the price one is willing to pay. Seasonal demand, economic conditions, and the seller’s circumstances all play a role. Sellers may be more open to negotiation if they are downsizing a collection or preparing for an estate sale. Conversely, rare items appearing during peak collecting seasons may command higher prices due to increased competition.  

Approaching negotiations with respect and knowledge of the item’s attributes can lead to a mutually agreeable price. Being prepared to walk away if the offer exceeds one’s valuation helps maintain discipline and ensures purchases remain aligned with collecting goals.

---

**Conclusion**  

Determining the right price for vintage weather observation instruments is an art that blends objective market research with subjective appreciation. By carefully weighing rarity, historical significance, condition, market comparisons, and personal value, collectors can make informed decisions that honor both the heritage of the instrument and their own collecting journey. Ultimately, the ideal price is one that reflects the instrument’s story and the collector’s passion, ensuring that each acquisition becomes a treasured part of the collection.

**Shaping the Curve: How Convex Design Trends Have Influenced Smartphones Over the Past Decade**  

Over the past ten years, the smartphone industry has undergone a quiet but significant transformation—one that is as much about the feel of a device in the hand as it is about the power within its circuitry. While technological advancements such as faster processors, improved cameras, and high‑resolution displays often dominate headlines, the evolution of design—particularly the embrace of convex forms—has played a pivotal role in shaping consumer preferences.  

### The Rise of Convex Aesthetics  

In the early 2010s, smartphone designs leaned heavily toward flat, slab‑like shapes. This was partly due to manufacturing simplicity and the prevailing minimalistic design philosophy. However, as competition intensified, manufacturers began experimenting with subtle curves, both in the body and the display. Convex backs, gently rounded edges, and ergonomic contours became increasingly common, offering a tactile appeal that flat designs lacked.  

Convex design elements serve multiple purposes. A curved back can make a large device feel slimmer and more comfortable to hold, while rounded corners contribute to a perception of softness and approachability in the product’s aesthetic. These features also help differentiate models visually, reinforcing brand identity in a crowded market.  

### Balancing Ergonomics and Engineering  

The shift toward convex forms presented engineers with new challenges. Internal components—battery cells, circuit boards, and cooling systems—are optimized for flat planes, so curving the chassis required innovations in component arrangement and manufacturing processes. For example, flexible printed circuit boards allowed designers to follow the contour of the device’s body, while advances in battery design enabled slight curvature without compromising capacity.  

Ergonomics became a central consideration. Studies in human‑device interaction revealed that convex surfaces distribute pressure more evenly across the palm, reducing hand fatigue during prolonged use. This insight prompted brands like Samsung and LG to introduce devices with pronounced curvature, such as the Galaxy Round and LG G Flex, which showcased how convexity could be both a visual and functional asset.  

### Case Studies from Leading Brands  

**Apple**: While Apple has traditionally favored minimalistic, flat designs, its iterative changes over the past decade have subtly incorporated convexity. The transition from the iPhone 5’s sharp edges to the iPhone 6’s rounded aluminum frame marked a turning point. More recent models have blended flat display panels with gently curved edges, balancing the crisp look of a flat screen with the comfortable grip of a convex frame.  

**Samsung**: Samsung’s design experimentation has been more overt. The Galaxy S6 Edge introduced a curved display that wrapped over the sides, merging aesthetic distinctiveness with practical features like edge notifications. Although not purely convex in the traditional sense, these curves influenced consumer perceptions of premium design and set a trend for immersive screen experiences.  

**Huawei**: Huawei’s flagship models, such as the Mate series, embraced convex back panels combined with high‑gloss finishes. This not only enhanced ergonomics but also reflected light in ways that accentuated color gradients, creating a sense of depth and luxury.  

### The Consumer Technology Preference Shift  

Convex design trends reflect a broader evolution in consumer priorities. As smartphone performance has plateaued in certain areas, design and feel have become more decisive factors in purchase decisions. Surveys from the past five years indicate that consumers increasingly describe “comfort in hand” and “premium feel” as key attributes influencing their choice. Convexity, by softening edges and improving ergonomics, aligns closely with these expectations.  

Moreover, convex designs often complement advancements in materials science. The move toward glass backs for wireless charging compatibility, for instance, has been paired with subtle curvature to improve durability and tactile appeal. Gorilla Glass and ceramic composites have made it possible to curve surfaces without sacrificing structural integrity.  

### Looking Ahead  

The next decade will likely see convexity evolve alongside emerging technologies. Foldable smartphones already challenge traditional form factors, and their flexible displays naturally lend themselves to curved surfaces. Manufacturers may also explore micro‑convex textures that improve grip without altering the overall silhouette, or adaptive convexity where the device’s shape can subtly shift for different usage modes.  

Ultimately, the embrace of convex design in smartphones is a testament to how aesthetics, ergonomics, and engineering can converge to meet consumer desires. It is a reminder that even as devices become more powerful, their physical form—how they feel, how they fit into our lives—remains central to their appeal. Convexity, with its blend of comfort and elegance, will likely continue to shape the way we hold the future in our hands.

**Abstract**  
Reverse purchase agreements (RPAs) have played a notable role in the development of European energy trading markets, particularly within the context of overnight electricity swaps. This paper traces the historical evolution of these instruments from their inception in the late 1990s to their current application as tools for managing supply-demand imbalances and stabilizing grid operations. By examining regulatory frameworks, market structures, and operational mechanisms, the study highlights the ways in which RPAs have been adapted to address the unique volatility of electricity markets, drawing parallels with broader financial market practices while emphasizing sector-specific innovations.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Electricity markets in Europe have undergone substantial liberalization over the past three decades, leading to the emergence of complex trading arrangements designed to handle inherent supply fluctuations. Among these arrangements, reverse purchase agreements—structured similarly to reverse repurchase agreements in financial markets—have been adapted to facilitate overnight electricity swaps. These contracts enable market participants to temporarily transfer electricity supply capacity in exchange for financial consideration, with a commitment to reverse the transaction within a short time frame, typically by the next day. The evolution of RPAs in this sector reflects both the increasing sophistication of market mechanisms and the persistent challenge of balancing supply and demand in real time.

---

**2. Historical Context**  
The origins of overnight electricity swaps in Europe can be traced to the deregulation initiatives of the late 1990s and early 2000s, particularly the European Union’s Electricity Directive (96/92/EC) and subsequent legislative measures. These reforms sought to introduce competition, increase cross-border trade, and improve operational efficiency. Initially, balancing mechanisms relied heavily on bilateral contracts and day-ahead markets. However, as intraday volatility became more pronounced—driven by variable renewable generation and fluctuating demand—market operators and participants began to adapt financial instruments such as RPAs to energy trading contexts [1].

In the early phases, RPAs were primarily used by large utilities and transmission system operators (TSOs) to secure short-term capacity from counterparties. The contractual structure mirrored financial reverse repos, with electricity supply acting as the underlying asset rather than securities. This allowed parties to address temporary shortages or surpluses without committing to long-term contractual obligations.

---

**3. Operational Mechanisms**  
An overnight electricity RPA typically involves two legs: the initial sale of electricity supply rights from one party to another, and the subsequent repurchase of those rights at a pre-agreed price on the following day. The pricing incorporates both the prevailing spot market rate and a premium reflecting the counterparty’s opportunity cost. In practice, these agreements are executed through centralized trading platforms or via over-the-counter (OTC) arrangements, depending on market segment and regulatory requirements.

The utility of RPAs in this context lies in their ability to provide immediate liquidity in supply capacity. For example, a generator facing an unexpected outage can procure electricity through an RPA to meet contractual delivery obligations, while a supplier with surplus generation can monetize excess capacity without committing to long-term sales. Settlement occurs in energy units (MWh) rather than in monetary form alone, with financial settlement mechanisms ensuring payment and delivery compliance [2].

---

**4. Role in Grid Stabilization**  
Overnight RPAs contribute to grid stability by facilitating rapid reallocation of supply resources. TSOs, tasked with maintaining frequency and voltage within acceptable limits, benefit from the availability of flexible instruments that can be activated outside the standard day-ahead and intraday markets. By enabling market participants to respond swiftly to unforeseen events—such as sudden drops in wind generation or spikes in demand—RPAs help reduce reliance on costly emergency reserves.

Moreover, the contractual certainty provided by RPAs enhances predictability in grid operations. Since counterparties commit to reversing the transaction within a fixed time frame, TSOs can factor these arrangements into short-term balancing strategies. This predictability mitigates the risk of prolonged imbalances that could threaten system integrity [3].

---

**5. Regulatory and Market Developments**  
The integration of RPAs into European electricity trading has been shaped by both national and EU-level regulations. Market transparency requirements, collateral provisions, and standardized contract forms have been introduced to reduce counterparty risk and improve market efficiency. The growth of centralized balancing markets, such as those operated by Nord Pool and EPEX SPOT, has further facilitated the use of RPAs by providing a common platform for execution and settlement.

Recent developments in renewable integration have intensified interest in overnight RPAs. As the proportion of variable generation sources increases, so too does the need for instruments that can manage short-term volatility. The European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) has recognized RPAs as one of several tools that can complement reserves and demand response measures in maintaining operational security [4].

---

**6. Conclusion**  
The historical trajectory of reverse purchase agreements in European electricity markets illustrates the adaptability of financial concepts to sector-specific requirements. Overnight electricity swaps, structured as RPAs, have emerged as valuable tools for managing supply fluctuations and stabilizing grid operations. Their continued relevance will likely depend on evolving market designs, regulatory environments, and the pace of renewable energy integration. As electricity systems become more dynamic, instruments that combine liquidity provision with operational flexibility are poised to remain integral to market stability.

---

**Physiological Mechanisms of Impression Formation: Neurobiological Processes in the Limbic System**  

---

**Abstract**  
Impression formation is a fundamental aspect of human social interaction, influencing interpersonal judgments and subsequent behaviors. This paper examines the physiological mechanisms underlying first impressions, with a particular emphasis on the neurobiological processes within the limbic system. Drawing on recent neuroscientific research, we explore how rapid affective evaluations are mediated by structures such as the amygdala, hippocampus, and orbitofrontal cortex, and how these regions integrate sensory input to produce coherent social assessments. We also discuss the role of neurotransmitters and hormonal modulators in shaping impression valence and intensity, and consider the implications for understanding bias, trust, and social decision-making.  

---

**1. Introduction**  
First impressions occur within milliseconds of an encounter and exert disproportionate influence over subsequent social judgments. Neurobiological evidence suggests that these rapid evaluations are driven by subcortical and cortical mechanisms that prioritize adaptive responses to novel social stimuli [1]. The limbic system, a network of interconnected structures involved in emotion, motivation, and memory, plays a central role in this process. By integrating multisensory information, the limbic system facilitates swift categorization of individuals as trustworthy, competent, threatening, or otherwise socially salient.  

---

**2. Limbic System Structures in Impression Formation**  

**2.1 Amygdala**  
The amygdala is critically involved in the detection and appraisal of emotional cues, particularly those related to threat or reward [2]. Functional imaging studies have shown that amygdala activation correlates with rapid judgments of facial trustworthiness and emotional expression. This activation occurs even before conscious recognition, suggesting that amygdala-mediated processes form the foundation of initial impressions by biasing attention toward salient social signals.  

**2.2 Hippocampus**  
While traditionally associated with memory consolidation, the hippocampus contributes to impression formation by contextualizing new encounters within existing social memories [3]. This contextualization enables individuals to compare current sensory input with stored representations, influencing the perceived familiarity or novelty of the other person. Such comparisons can modulate affective responses and the strength of the initial impression.  

**2.3 Orbitofrontal Cortex (OFC)**  
The OFC integrates affective signals from the amygdala with sensory and contextual information from other brain regions. This integration supports evaluative judgments that balance emotional reactions with learned social norms [4]. OFC activity is implicated in updating impressions based on new information, allowing for the refinement of initial assessments over time.  

---

**3. Neurochemical Modulation**  
Neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine influence the processing speed and valence of impressions. Dopaminergic signaling in reward pathways can enhance positive evaluations, while serotonergic modulation contributes to impulse control and regulation of negative affect [5]. Hormonal factors, including oxytocin and cortisol, further impact impression formation; oxytocin is associated with increased trust and empathy, whereas elevated cortisol levels can heighten vigilance and bias judgments toward caution.  

---

**4. Sensory Integration and Rapid Processing**  
First impressions rely on the rapid integration of visual, auditory, and olfactory cues. Visual processing of facial features engages the fusiform face area, which communicates with limbic structures to associate perceived traits with emotional significance. Auditory cues, such as tone of voice, are processed in the superior temporal gyrus and linked to affective appraisal via amygdala connections. Olfactory signals, though often subconscious, can evoke strong emotional responses through direct projections to the limbic system, bypassing the thalamic relay [6].  

---

**5. Implications for Social Interaction**  
Understanding the physiological mechanisms behind impression formation provides insight into phenomena such as bias, stereotyping, and trust development. The limbic system’s rapid evaluations can be adaptive in situations requiring quick decisions, yet they may also lead to persistent inaccuracies when initial impressions are resistant to change. By recognizing the neural substrates of these processes, researchers and practitioners can better address the ways in which unconscious affective responses shape interpersonal and group dynamics.  

---

**6. Conclusion**  
First impressions are the product of complex neurobiological interactions within the limbic system, integrating sensory input with emotional and contextual information. The amygdala, hippocampus, and orbitofrontal cortex, modulated by neurochemical and hormonal influences, work in concert to produce swift, affectively charged judgments that guide social behavior. Continued investigation into these processes holds promise for advancing our understanding of human social cognition and improving strategies for mitigating maladaptive biases.  

---

**References**

[2] Adolphs, R. (2010). What does the amygdala contribute to social cognition? *Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences*, 1191, 42–61.

**I. Overview**

Figure 4 Categorizing Shareholders to Dissect their Heterogeneous Influence on Stakeholders
Related to our typology, the literature also reveals four channels through which shareholders can influence stakeholders: (1) Voice and exit occurs when shareholders exert influence by threatening to sell their shares (exit) or actively expressing their preferences to managers (voice)—for instance, by filing shareholder proposals or meeting privately with management; (2) ownership signaling manifests from the presence of certain shareholders sending signals that affect managerial decision-making and firm outcomes. For instance, shares held by politicians can signal political support for the respective firm and influence corporate lobbying activities (Ridge et al., 2018), whereas ownership by activist investors can send a signal of shareholder discontentment to management of nontargeted firms (Shi, Connelly, Hoskisson, & Ketchen, 2019); (3) resource provision refers to the resources shareholders provide that influence stakeholder interests. Such resources include access to financing (Phillips & Sertsios, 2017), knowledge sharing (Connelly, Lee, Tihanyi, Certo, & Johnson, 2019), and legitimacy (Marquis & Qian, 2014); 4 and (4) direct decision-making describes the situation that shareholders make the decisions themselves, rather than use tactics to influence the decisions of managers from the outside (as with the other three channels), because firms are owned and directly managed by one dominant shareholder. Typical examples are family-owned firms and firms that are majority-owned by private-equity investors. As we will show, the four types of shareholders we classify utilize these four channels of influence in different ways. Importantly, these channels are not mutually exclusive, so the same shareholder may use multiple channels to influence management. For example, shareholders filing proposals can voice their preferences to managers through proposals while also sending a signal to managers of nontargeted firms (Reid & Toffel, 2009).
Shareholder Types and Stakeholder Interests
In this section, we discuss in detail each of the four quadrants of Figure 4, which we derived from our typology. We assigned the types of shareholders discussed in each study to one or more quadrants according to the authors’ assumptions about them. Some types of shareholders have been assigned to multiple quadrants, depending on those assumptions.5
Transactional Ownership: Short-Term Financial Shareholders
Transactional shareholders (Figure 4, upper-left quadrant) seek to maximize financial returns over a short period, with little concern for nonfinancial goals. As high portfolio turnover tends to reflect a short horizon, it is often captured in studies examining “transient” investors (see the classification by Bushee, 1998) with prominent financial objectives. Some of the reviewed studies examine specific subtypes of this category of shareholders, such as financially driven activist hedge funds (DesJardine, Marti, & Durand, 2021) and activist short sellers (Shi & DesJardine, 2022). Transactional shareholders trade in and out of stocks relatively quickly to maximize the financial performance of their portfolios and discount future earnings more drastically than longer-term shareholders.
Impacts on stakeholders. The literature is clear that transactional shareholders orient managers to initiatives that elevate short-term earnings and shareholder wealth above objectives that are more relevant to stakeholders. This approach can result in intense corporate cost cutting (Cobb, 2015; DesJardine & Durand, 2020) and cash redistributions where capital is allocated back to shareholders through stock repurchases or dividends (Boyson & Mooradian, 2011; Klein & Zur, 2011).
With regard to stakeholders, several studies show that transactional ownership hurts employees by reducing employment security and job prospects. Transactional shareholders can levy pressure on managers to reduce growth and transfer resources from employees to shareholders. Lin (2016) found that managers do this by replacing permanent employees with contract workers as ownership by transactional institutional shareholders increases. Antoni, Maug, and Obernberger (2019) reported that establishments reduce their workforce by about 9% following a private equity buyout and that job losses mostly affect employees who are least likely to find work elsewhere—arguably the most vulnerable. Likewise, ownership by transactional activist hedge funds can reduce firm growth and result in job losses (DesJardine & Durand, 2020), some of which are voluntary due to the depressed job prospects and workplace culture that the retained employees encounter (Chen, Meyer-Doyle, & Shi, 2021). Ahmadjian and Robbins (2005) argued that transactional foreign investors place little value on long-term employment security and instigate significant downsizing and job losses; David, O’brien, Yoshikawa, and Delios (2010) further confirmed these findings.
Transactional ownership can also lead to reductions in the pay and benefits of employees. A broad array of transactional shareholders, including but not limited to activist hedge funds (Agrawal & Lim, 2021), can lead companies to reduce their pension benefits for employees, especially when the shareholders are actively involved in corporate affairs (Cobb, 2015). Such shareholders can also flatten employees’ pay and work hours (e.g., Brav, Jiang, & Kim, 2015) and even increase employee injury and illness rates (Shi, Xia, & Meyer-Doyle, 2021). Providing one estimate of the financial cost to employees, Antoni et al. (2019) found that the average employee loses €980 in annual earnings following a private equity buyout.
Focusing on transactional shareholders, Liu et al. (2014) provided survey evidence that higher share turnover induces managers to invest less in employee-oriented human resource systems. Connelly, Haynes, Tihanyi, Gamache, and Devers (2016) found that such losses can benefit managers; specifically, the authors found that transactional ownership increases management-to-worker pay dispersion, whereby managers earn more as employees earn less.
Assuming the development of new and innovative products benefits customers, transactional ownership may also harm customer interests by impeding corporate R&D and product development efforts. Bushee (1998) was among the first to show that ownership by short-term transactional shareholders reduces firm R&D. Hoskisson, Hitt, Johnson, and Grossman (2002) found that professional fund managers, whose orientation, they argue, is transactional, pressure managers to focus on acquiring other businesses so as to quickly expand their product offerings, rather than taking the more time-consuming path of organically developing new products and innovating within the firm. Likewise, Zahra (1996) found that transactional institutional ownership leads companies away from internal product development and time-consuming and risky corporate entrepreneurship activities. Similarly, Chan, Chen, Chen, and Yu (2015) observed that firms with a high level of transactional ownership are prompted to avoid earnings surprises by reducing their R&D and advertising costs. As an exception, Giannetti and Yu (2021) concluded that transactional ownership can help firms adapt to changes in their industry's environment by introducing more new products and trademarks.
Transactional shareholders may also have a negative impact on the broader community—for example, by encouraging corporate tax avoidance (Chen, Huang, Li, & Shevlin, 2019; Cheng, Huang, Li, & Stanfield, 2012; Khan, Srinivasan, & Tan, 2017), which may hurt local governments and their citizens. In the context of education, Eaton, Howell, and Yannelis (2020) reported that schools owned by private equity prioritize short-term profits, which leads to lower education inputs, graduation rates, loan repayment rates, and earnings among school graduates. In a different context, Klein and Zur (2011) showed that transactional activist ownership increases company leverage and cash redistributions at the expense of creditors.
Several studies indicate that transactional shareholders can undermine corporate social responsibility (CSR), potentially harming the welfare of a broad range of stakeholders and the natural environment. DesJardine and Durand (2020) found that companies whose ownership passes largely to transactional activist hedge funds reduce their CSR activities, in line with the earlier findings of Neubaum and Zahra (2006) that transactional institutional ownership reduces CSR. Looking at specific subdimensions of CSR, Johnson and Greening (1999) showed that companies owned by transactional investment managers reduce CSR efforts oriented toward people (e.g., communities, women and minorities, and employees) and products.
Overall, research shows that the influence transactional shareholders exercise on their portfolio companies almost invariably has a negative impact on a broad array of stakeholders. By prioritizing the short-term maximization of shareholder wealth, transactional ownership seems to orient managers toward decisions that overlook the interests of other stakeholders. Of all stakeholders, employees suffer the most; however, transactional ownership may have a negative impact also on customers, communities, and creditors.
Channels of influence. According to existing research, transactional shareholders influence firm activities largely by becoming involved in the decision-making process of corporate executives through voice and exit. Most papers in this strand discuss broadly the “pressures” transactional shareholders place on managers (e.g., DesJardine & Durand, 2020: 1060; Lin, 2016: 978; Liu et al., 2014: 427), whom they “encourage” (Hoskisson et al., 2002: 700; Neubaum & Zahra, 2006: 112) or “push” (Yoshikawa, Phan, & David, 2005: 283) to pursue certain strategies that favor these shareholders’ short-term financial interests. For example, scholars argue that transactional shareholders can “motivate executives to engage in actions that enhance short-term earnings” (Cobb, 2015: 1337) and limit managers’ discretion to pursue objectives that fall outside the narrow profit-maximization window (Connelly, Shi, & Zyung, 2017). As managers do not want to disappoint transactional shareholders with low earnings, they will sometimes take excessive measures to boost short-term profits, even at the expense of long-term value and the welfare of the firm's stakeholders (Liu et al., 2014).
Other studies argue that transactional shareholders influence firm outcomes by selling their holdings when their interests are not met (e.g., Zahra, 1996). Some of these studies indicate that transactional shareholders apply both the mechanisms of “exit” (i.e., sell-offs) and “voice” (e.g., private meetings with management), whereas other studies (e.g., Bushee, 1998) suggest that the timespan over which they hold stock is so short that such investors are precluded from voicing their concerns to management, making exit the main influence channel (e.g., Connelly, Tihanyi, et al., 2010).
Theoretical foundations. Agency theory (Eisenhardt, 1989) provides the most commonly used theoretical scaffolding for understanding how transactional ownership influences stakeholder-related corporate activities. The basic assumption underlying agency theory is that managers (i.e., agents) will at times pursue their own interests at the expense of shareholders (i.e., principals). Some studies (e.g., Masulis & Reza, 2015) that follow this assumption posit that managers who distribute corporate resources so as to advance stakeholder welfare pursue their own interests at the expense of transactional shareholders. For instance, Atkinson and Galaskiewicz (1988: 86) argued that “agent-managers are more likely than owners to give money away to charity, because they have no direct claim on residual earnings.” Other studies (e.g., Yoshikawa et al., 2005) examine the role of transactional shareholders in principal–principal conflicts, which arise from differences in risk preferences and investment objectives between transactional shareholders and other types of shareholders. The principal–principal theoretical lens offers a promising tool for unpacking conflicts between transactional shareholders and other investors, and how those conflicts implicate stakeholders.
Overall, however, agency theory provides a somewhat simplistic view of the relation between transactional shareholders and managers, whose decisions implicate other stakeholders. The view that managers are inherently inclined to attend to stakeholder interests for self-serving reasons and are only restrained by transactional shareholders, who serve primarily the financial interests of the corporation, seems to conflict with research on the complexity of stakeholder management and financial returns. For example, Flammer and Kacperczyk (2016) find that attending to stakeholder interests can help companies innovate in ways that propel long-term financial performance. To better understand when transactional shareholders can have a positive impact on stakeholders, research would benefit from refreshing agency theory with new theories based on different assumptions about managerial self-interest or the factors that curtail it, such as stewardship theory (Davis, Schoorman, & Donaldson, 2018) or upper echelons theory (Hambrick & Mason, 1984).
Durable Investment: Long-Term Financial Shareholders
Durable shareholders (Figure 4, upper-right quadrant) aim to maximize financial returns over a long horizon, with limited concern for nonfinancial outcomes. As low portfolio turnover rates (i.e., churn rates) reflect long horizons, “dedicated” shareholders (Bushee, 1998) are classified as “durable” when they primarily seek financial returns. Pension funds (Johnson & Greening, 1999) that are mostly motivated by the financial performance of their portfolios may fit this classification, depending on the institutional context. Large owners, such as blockholding index investors, may also have long horizons, as their significant holdings make it hard to efficiently divest their shares (DesJardine, Grewal, & Viswanathan, forthcoming). Large holdings tie investors to the respective firms and, as Lee and O’Neill (2003: 215) put it, “[this] mutual dependence creates a long-term relationship between investors and managers.” Some studies argue that, because of their long horizons, durable shareholders may be more sensitive to the risk of negative corporate externalities and, as a result, may be motivated to engage companies on stakeholder-relevant issues purely for financial reasons (e.g., DesJardine et al., forthcoming).
Impacts on stakeholders. Long horizons lead durable shareholders to pay close attention to the delayed financial returns that result from some forms of corporate investment, as is likely in the case of stakeholder-oriented and CSR initiatives (Bansal & DesJardine, 2014). Positioning pension funds as durable shareholders, Johnson and Greening (1999) argued that these shareholders’ long horizons incline managers to invest in stakeholder-related activities in order to reap potential long-term benefits of those investments. In sum, in contrast to the shorter horizons of transactional shareholders, the long horizons of durable shareholders might temper the negative effects of their purely financial objectives on stakeholder interests.
If transactional shareholders harm employee interests, one might suspect durable shareholders have the opposite effect. This is indeed evident in some instances but not in others. Scholars have shown that durable shareholders can offset the pecuniary losses employees suffer because of transactional owners (Cobb, 2015) and soften the negative impact that analyst earnings pressures can have on corporate downsizing (Schulz & Wiersema, 2018). Connelly et al. (2016) found that durable ownership by dedicated institutional shareholders reduces pay dispersion between managers and employees and fosters more equal pay practices in organizations. Other studies indicate that durable foreign owners generally support new corporate investment in human capital (Bena, Ferreira, Matos, & Pires, 2017). However, Jung (2016) found that the presence of financially driven dedicated institutional investors intensifies downsizing and therefore reduces job security for employees.
Durable shareholders can serve the interests of customers insofar as they facilitate firm innovation and corporate entrepreneurial pursuits. For example, the negative impact of a reduced takeover threat on innovation is relatively limited for companies with durable shareholders (Atanassov, 2013). There is also evidence that, because durable shareholders expect long-term share appreciation, they generally support corporate R&D activities (Chowdhury & Geringer, 2001; David, Hitt, & Gimeno, 2001; Hansen & Hill, 1991). Hoskisson et al. (2002) showed that durable pension funds—motivated by long-term financial returns—facilitate internal innovation, rather than pushing managers to acquire innovation externally for quicker results. In a cross-national study, Lee and O’Neill (2003) found that blockholding durable shareholders bolster corporate R&D efforts in the United States but not in Japan, where, they argue, the interests of managers better align with those of long-term blockholders.
Some studies suggest that durable shareholders may also promote CSR efforts and environmental outcomes. Neubaum and Zahra (2006) found that holdings by long-term institutional shareholders are significantly and positively associated with a firm's CSR; more so when the shareholders use activist tactics to intervene in corporate decision-making. More recently, Chen, Dong, and Lin (2020: 496) found evidence supporting their claim that institutions with “long-term investment horizons are the main force to drive CSR improvement”; however, the authors did not directly measure the sampled investors’ orientation. It is possible that more conclusive evidence would arise from research on specific types of shareholders that can be classified as “durable.” Kacperczyk (2009), for instance, argued that the long horizons of financially oriented pension funds motivate them to pressure firms to attend to the interests of other stakeholders, which results in observable increases in CSR activities. Similarly, analyses of specific subdimensions of CSR indicate that durable shareholders can improve the environment and the welfare of communities (e.g., Johnson & Greening, 1999). Recently, Azar, Duro, Kadach, and Ormazabal (2021) showed that ownership by the “Big Three”—BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street—which they position as durable shareholders, leads to reductions in the owned firms’ annual carbon emissions. The authors argue that these shareholders benefit from pushing for a reduction of emissions because doing so makes their investment vehicles more attractive to a broader class of socially minded clients. Taking a different view, DesJardine et al. (forthcoming) found causal evidence that long-term common owners enhance the CSR performance of their portfolio firms in order to promote financially material positive spillovers between firms’ CSR activities.
Durable investment can also promote transparency in a firm's stakeholder-related activities. Arguing that investors with long horizons are likely to view philanthropy as a form of investment, Wang et al. (2021) found evidence that financially motivated institutional investors with long horizons mitigate the concerns of managers that investors will view corporate philanthropic activities negatively. As a result, managers become more open to publicizing such initiatives. By comparison, Shi, Connelly, and Hoskisson (2017) argue that the durable shareholders’ direct oversight of corporate activities reduces managers’ intrinsic motivation to act ethically. This, the authors found, tends to increase corporate financial fraud, which, in severe cases, can harm not only governments and creditors but also a range of stakeholders whose welfare depends on an organization (e.g., employees or communities). Overall, in contrast to the effects of transactional shareholders on stakeholders, those of durable investors can be positive or negative, depending on the circumstances and context.
Channels of influence. Prior studies suggest that durable shareholders intervene in corporate decision-making largely by providing managers with more discretion in day-to-day decisions. Only a minority of studies (e.g., Kacperczyk, 2009) speak of shareholders pressuring or coercing managers to take specific decisions. Most works assume that the objectives and preferences of durable shareholders align more naturally with those of management, and it is through this alignment that durable shareholders influence managers (e.g., Schulz & Wiersema, 2018). This assumption implies that managers have long horizons at any rate and that durable capital gives them the freedom to do what they would naturally do if they were not subject to the pressures of myopic capital markets. David et al. (2010), for instance, argued that durable shareholders allow managers and employees considerable discretion as to how to utilize the firm's resources (also see Connelly, Tihanyi, Ketchen, Carnes, & Ferrier, 2017). More recent works suggest that durable investment can make managers “feel less threatened” in general (Oehmichen et al., 2021: 6) and less sensitive (Schulz & Wiersema, 2018) to myopic investment pressures (Zhang & Gimeno, 2016).
Some studies, however, argue that while durable shareholders may shield managers from other pressures, at the same time they influence managers by intensely monitoring managerial activities (Connelly, Tihanyi, et al., 2010). Other works suggest that monitoring—at least when mostly passive—does not afford durable institutional shareholders sufficient force to influence managers. Rather such shareholders need to use their voice to motivate management (Chen et al., 2020; David et al., 2001). In sum, some studies assume that durable shareholders influence managers by adopting a hands-off approach and relieving them of pressures from capital markets and other shareholders, whereas others assume that direct intervention is a precondition for shareholder influence.
Some scholars argue that durable shareholders are an important information source for managers. Because of their typically long investment horizon, durable shareholders have the experience and willingness to share their insights and ideas with the managers of their portfolio companies. For example, according to Connelly, Tihanyi, et al. (2010), these shareholders have special knowledge, which they accumulate by holding shares for long periods. Building on this view, Boh, Huang, and Wu (2020) argued that experienced and patient durable shareholders can assist firms with environmental scanning and promote innovation by providing relevant industry information. Where relevant, such information might influence the trade-offs managers make between the interests of shareholders and other stakeholders. In this vein, Oehmichen et al. (2021) suggested that the information durable shareholders provide could be especially useful in areas where evaluating outcomes is difficult, such as CSR.
Theoretical foundations. Like many works on transactional shareholders, studies on durable shareholders rely heavily on agency theory. As a result of their long investment horizons and intense monitoring, durable shareholders provide managers with more discretion to invest in stakeholders, if such investments are expected to increase long-term shareholder value (Bena et al., 2017). Based on this premise, some studies assume that stakeholder engagement promotes the long-term financial value of the firm (e.g., David et al., 2001). Another common assumption is that durable shareholders are more capable of collecting and processing information than other types of shareholders (e.g., Lee & O’Neill, 2003). According to this view, the reduced information asymmetry enables durable shareholders to distinguish more accurately the self-interested pursuits that agency theory assumes managers have from well-intentioned investments in stakeholder welfare that aim to maximize long-term financial performance (Oehmichen et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). As a result, even though durable shareholders prioritize financial returns, their involvement in corporate affairs can, at times, benefit other stakeholders.
Another stream of research on durable shareholders relies on a set of behavioral theories, including the behavioral theory of the firm and cognitive evaluation theory (Shi et al., 2017). According to these behavioral theories, managerial decision-making is influenced by external stimuli, such as earnings pressures and shareholder expectations (e.g., Schulz & Wiersema, 2018). Durable shareholders can either soften or amplify the effects such stimuli have on managers and thus alter how managers decide on activities related to stakeholders. For instance, although managers may feel pressured to downsize when firm performance falls short of analysts’ expectations, institutional shareholders with a long-term outlook can relieve managers of these pressures (Schulz & Wiersema, 2018).
As theoretical tools, behavioral theories help explain the tendencies and biases that find their way into managerial decision-making amid shareholder pressures and can therefore usefully complement research in this stream. However, few studies formally integrate behavioral theories with other theories that have been traditionally used to understand the influence of shareholders, such as agency theory (Eisenhardt, 1989) and stewardship theory (Davis et al., 2018). To provide a comprehensive account of how shareholders in general influence stakeholders, as well as deeper insights into how durable shareholders in particular influence managerial decision-making, research would benefit from integrating behavioral and nonbehavioral theories, rather than taking an “either/or” approach.
Purpose-Driven Ownership: Short-Term Multipurpose Shareholders
Purpose-driven shareholders (Figure 4, bottom-left quadrant) have short horizons over which they seek to accomplish financial and nonfinancial objectives, including prosocial outcomes. Of all four types, these shareholders are the rarest in the literature because there are relatively few of them to study before the 2010s, which is when the number of shareholder activists and shareholder resolutions with social objectives started to accelerate. Despite their rarity, as scant academic and anecdotal evidence suggests, such shareholders can have real effects on stakeholder-relevant corporate activities, making them worth review.
Impacts on stakeholders. Although there is an extensive literature on the effects of shareholder proposals on environmental and social outcomes, it is hard to verify that such proposals have been filed by shareholders with short horizons. Few studies make explicit assumptions about the types of shareholders who file such proposals, including whether they have short or long horizons. One exception is the study by Flammer, Toffel, and Viswanathan (2021), who found that shareholder proposals on environmental and social issues filed by institutional investors with short-term horizons promote climate-change disclosure less effectively than proposals filed by long-term institutional investors. Other studies, which do not look at the specific horizons of the filers, report mixed findings on the effectiveness of environmental and social shareholder resolutions. David et al. (2007) observed that such proposals filed by shareholders can divert resources away from CSR and into managerial political efforts to resist external pressures and retain discretion. On the other hand, McDonnell, King, and Soule (2015) argued that environmental and social shareholder proposals can lead firms to introduce CSR reporting and establish CSR committees, which can have positive long-term consequences for firms and their stakeholders. Whether proposal activism undermines or promotes CSR seems to depend on the type and horizon of shareholders who file proposals.
Another type of purpose-driven shareholder is the socially oriented or ESG (environmental-social-governance) activist hedge fund. Activist hedge funds have historically focused only on maximizing financial returns and increasingly use their ownership positions to achieve financially material sustainability objectives. Because these investors tend to have very short horizons, but can have considerable impacts on corporate priorities and activities (DesJardine & Durand, 2020), they present a formidable type of purpose-driven shareholder. Although several working papers are currently exploring the effects of purpose-driven activist hedge funds (e.g., Chu & Zhao, 2019), researchers need to investigate more campaigns to derive empirically robust insights.
Channels of influence. Purpose-driven shareholders have relatively limited channels of influence on corporate practices and policies, largely because they do not have the necessary time to engage patiently in dialogue with managers nor, in many cases, the capital needed to build a position large enough for them to leverage a credible threat of exit, if their nonfinancial interests are not met. Therefore, a common tactic of these shareholders is to expose other shareholders to nonfinancial issues in a company, intending that those shareholders have the power to elicit a substantive response by managers (e.g., McDonnell et al., 2015). One obvious channel purpose-driven shareholders use to that end is the shareholder proposal (or resolution; Flammer et al., 2021). Some social movement organizations have built in-house activist investing divisions that acquire stockholdings to submit proposals aiming to achieve their social objectives.
As activist hedge funds begin to focus more on social and environmental issues in their campaigns, they gain access to new channels of influence. As noted earlier, activist hedge funds have short horizons but also deep financial reservoirs that they can leverage to build significant positions in target companies. For instance, six months after launching its campaign against ExxonMobil in December 2020, the ESG-oriented activist hedge fund Engine No. 1 was able to appoint three of the four directors it had proposed to the company's board, with the aim to transform Exxon into a more environmentally sensitive oil conglomerate (DesJardine & Bansal, 2021). Obtaining board representation is unlikely to be feasible for many other types of purpose-driven shareholders. In contrast, activist hedge funds inclined to pursue environmental and social ends are more likely to be able to enjoy privileged access to new channels of influence—a possibility that opens up an exciting avenue for future study.
Theoretical foundations. Social movement theory dominates studies examining the influence of purpose-driven shareholders on firm outcomes. According to this theory, shareholders can use “private politics”—or nonmarket interactions with companies—to influence corporate actions related to the interests of other stakeholders (Reid & Toffel, 2009). As social movement theory emphasizes the characteristics of the corporate agent, it seems particularly useful in explaining how firms differ in their responses to social movements and therefore shedding light on the influence of purpose-driven shareholders. However, as research on purpose-driven shareholders remains limited, future studies will need to apply a broad array of theoretical lenses to unpack the effects these shareholders have on different stakeholders.
Sustainable Investment: Long-Term Multipurpose Shareholders
Sustainable shareholders (Figure 4, bottom-right quadrant) integrate nonfinancial criteria into their long-term investment objectives. Such shareholders consider financial returns from a more balanced perspective than other types of shareholders. Importantly, the category of sustainable shareholders is not limited to the classic types of long-term investors who have been included in this quadrant because of their socioeconomic and multigenerational objectives—that is, investors who focus on ESG or socially responsible investing (SRI) objectives and family owners (Gomez-Mejia et al., 2011). For instance, government shareholders will also be included in this category when they approach companies with a sustainable investment orientation. Fiss and Zajac (2006: 1177) argue that some government shareholders “have to attend to the interests of several corporate stakeholders.” Some foreign institutional shareholders will also fall into this quadrant when they approach local companies from a global ESG perspective, as will universal owners with “long-term fiduciary responsibilities to their customers, beneficiaries, and the wider community” (Dimson, Karakaş, & Li, 2015: 3226).
Impacts on stakeholders. The general view in the literature is that sustainable investment benefits stakeholders, especially employees. Numerous studies have shown that socially minded family shareholders with long horizons help their companies improve employee welfare—for instance, by treating employees better (Kang & Kim, 2020), decreasing the likelihood of lay-offs (Greenwood, Díaz, Li, & Lorente, 2010), and thus increasing job protection. Through their survey, Mullins and Schoar (2016: 24) found evidence that CEOs “feel more accountable to employees and banks than to shareholders” when family shareholders are involved in the company, which suggests that sustainable shareholders could improve employee welfare in a company by influencing the CEO's sentiment. Miller, Breton-Miller, and Scholnick (2008) found that sustainable family investment can help companies develop more employee-friendly practices by training workers better, making broader use of their skills, and being more flexible and inclusive. Whether these improvements in employee welfare arise because they “provide emotional and social benefits to the controlling family” (Miller, Le Breton-Miller, & Lester, 2013: 189) or because firms with higher family ownership have long time horizons and face low market pressure (Kang & Kim, 2020), it is evident that employees accrue multifaceted benefits from sustainable investment.
Sustainable investment may benefit a broad range of stakeholders, as well as the natural environment. Kim, Wan, Wang, and Yang (2019) found that sustainable shareholders, such as SRI funds, public pension funds, and dedicated institutional investors, help reduce the toxic emissions of facilities to which they are closely located. In an earlier study, Berrone, Cruz, Gomez-Mejia, and Larraza-Kintana (2010) showed that sustainable family investment can help firms reduce their negative environmental impacts.
Sustainable foreign shareholders can also improve stakeholder welfare in areas where local firms fall short of global standards regarding specific issues. Mun and Jung (2018: 412) argued, “The growth of foreign institutional ownership has put new pressure on Japanese firms to embrace global CSR standards . . . particularly regarding gender diversity, given that Japanese firms fall far behind their global competitors on the issue.” However, as other research indicates, context matters. Yoshikawa et al. (2005) found that domestic sustainable shareholders improve employee welfare by increasing compensation and promoting employee development. In some contrast, Dyck, Lins, Roth, and Wagner (2019) reasoned that among sustainable shareholders, only those who originate in countries with strong community beliefs in the importance of environmental and social issues will increase a firm's environmental and social performance.
Surprisingly, despite the benefits sustainable shareholders create for a range of stakeholders, they may sometimes harm customers. Boh et al. (2020) observed that, because sustainable family shareholders emphasize control and influence over-invested firms, they undermine firm innovation. Other studies have found that, because sustainable family shareholders tend to be risk averse and avoid innovative experiments that may lead to failure, they put pressure on their firms to reduce R&D efforts (Chrisman & Patel, 2012; Duran, Kammerlander, Van Essen, & Zellweger, 2016) and new product development (Souder, Zaheer, Sapienza, & Ranucci, 2017).
Channels of influence. Existing research suggests that sustainable shareholders often use voice to influence corporations regarding nonfinancial issues. Examining a single case study of ESG activism, Dimson et al. (2015) concluded that sustainable shareholders actively engage in dialogue with target companies, vote at shareholder meetings, screen out irresponsible companies, and partner with other sustainable shareholders and NGOs. By employing various tactics, such as screening (Vasudeva, 2013) and filing proposals (Kim et al., 2019), sustainable shareholders can exert “normative pressure on companies to adopt CSR practices” (Mun & Jung, 2018: 412). Private engagement, as the findings of Dyck et al. (2019) suggest, is the most effective channel through which sustainable shareholders can drive changes in stakeholder-relevant corporate activities.
Theoretical foundations. Studies on sustainable shareholders are often based on institutional theory, which asserts that organizations are not influenced exclusively by efficiency objectives but also by taken-for-granted norms, values, and logics that permeate the boundaries of business (Greenwood, Oliver, Sahlin, & Suddaby, 2008). Shareholders who are embedded in different institutional fields are thus exposed to different sets of values and belief systems that define legitimated practices. The long-term horizons and nonfinancial interests of sustainable shareholders can therefore orient managers toward improving their firms’ social responsibility and bearing the cost of pursuing pro-stakeholder actions (Greenwood et al., 2010). Although there is risk that investments in stakeholders do not produce financial returns, research shows that the preferences of sustainable shareholders are sometimes “driven by a belief that such a risk is counterbalanced by noneconomic utilities” (Berrone et al., 2010: 89).
Although institutional theory is useful for speculating about the broader pressures that can elicit change in organizations, its macro lens can miss the finer-grained channels through which sustainable shareholders engage companies on the ground. As research on the growing population of sustainable shareholders proliferates, scholars will need to integrate theories that unpack the dynamics between the sustainable shareholder, manager, and ecosystem of other actors.
An Agenda for Future Research
In this study, we reviewed cross-disciplinary research on the influence that shareholders have on stakeholder interests. Based on our review, we identified three overarching gaps in the literature, which now lead us to call for research that (1) explores the influence that different types of shareholders can have on stakeholders, (2) identifies new channels through which shareholders influence stakeholders, and (3) accounts for the interactive dynamics among shareholders and stakeholders. **The Geometric Principles of Medieval Cathedral Layouts: Proportion, Symmetry, and Symbolism in Architectural Design**  

---

**Abstract**  
This paper examines the architectural geometry of cathedral layouts in medieval Europe, with particular attention to the proportional systems, symmetrical arrangements, and symbolic design elements employed by master builders between the 11th and 15th centuries. Drawing on surviving architectural plans, extant structures, and contemporary treatises, the study situates cathedral geometry within broader intellectual currents, including scholastic thought, numerology, and theological symbolism. The analysis reveals how geometric planning served both functional and spiritual purposes, producing edifices that embodied cosmic order while accommodating liturgical practice.  

---

**Introduction**  
Medieval cathedrals stand as enduring monuments to the synthesis of engineering, artistry, and theology. Their ground plans and elevations are not merely products of pragmatic construction but deliberate applications of geometric principles imbued with symbolic meaning. The period from the Romanesque to the High Gothic saw a refinement of these principles, influenced by ancient sources such as Vitruvius and augmented by the scholastic emphasis on rational order [1]. This paper investigates the specific proportional and symmetrical systems underlying cathedral designs, with a focus on how master builders orchestrated spatial relationships to reflect theological concepts.  

---

**Proportional Systems**  
One of the most salient features of medieval cathedral geometry is the use of harmonic proportions. Builders often employed ratios derived from simple integers—such as 1:2, 2:3, and 3:4—to determine the relationships between nave width, transept length, and choir dimensions [2]. These ratios were believed to correspond to musical consonances, thereby linking architectural space to the medieval cosmology in which geometry and music were manifestations of divine order.  

Evidence from the floor plans of Chartres, Reims, and Salisbury indicates that the nave bays frequently conformed to a modular system, in which a single bay dimension served as the unit for the entire plan. This modularity facilitated both construction and symbolic coherence, with the repeated unit reinforcing the notion of unity within multiplicity.  

---

**Symmetry and Orientation**  
Symmetry in cathedral layouts was not merely an aesthetic choice but a theological statement. Bilateral symmetry along the longitudinal axis was ubiquitous, reflecting the medieval perception of the church as a microcosm of divine creation, ordered and balanced [3]. The axial alignment of the nave toward the east—symbolizing resurrection and the coming of Christ—further underscored the interplay between geometric order and spiritual meaning.  

In plan view, the cruciform arrangement of nave and transept constituted a central organizing geometry, with the crossing often serving as the focal point from which proportional relationships radiated. The placement of subsidiary chapels, cloisters, and portals adhered to geometric constraints that maintained visual and spatial balance.  

---

**Symbolic Geometry**  
Beyond proportion and symmetry, cathedral geometry incorporated symbolic forms such as circles, squares, and equilateral triangles. The circle, often manifest in rose windows and apsidal terminations, signified eternity and divine perfection. The square, used in choir and cloister layouts, represented the earthly realm, stability, and the four cardinal virtues. Triangular forms, particularly equilateral triangles, were imbued with Trinitarian symbolism, appearing in vaulting patterns and façade compositions [4].  

The integration of these forms was not incidental. Builders consciously embedded them into the structural and decorative schema, creating a layered visual language that communicated theological truths to the faithful, even if only subconsciously apprehended.  

---

**Case Studies**  
At Chartres Cathedral, geometric analysis reveals that the nave’s length is precisely twice its width, a ratio that aligns with the diapason in medieval music theory. The radial chapels of the apse are spaced according to equal angular divisions, producing a harmonious circular procession around the choir.  

Reims Cathedral exhibits a sophisticated interplay of vertical and horizontal proportions, with the height of the nave arcade relating to the clerestory in a 3:2 ratio. The façade’s tripartite division mirrors the interior’s three-aisle arrangement, reinforcing the unity of exterior and interior geometry.  

---

**Conclusion**  
Medieval cathedral geometry reflects a confluence of technical skill, mathematical knowledge, and theological intent. The proportional systems ensured structural integrity while resonating with contemporary conceptions of cosmic harmony. Symmetry and orientation reinforced the sacred function of the building, and symbolic forms embedded in the design communicated complex theological ideas through spatial experience. Understanding these geometric principles not only enriches our appreciation of medieval architecture but also illuminates the intellectual and spiritual milieu from which these monumental works emerged.  

---

[2] Bork, R. *The Geometry of Creation: Architectural Drawing and the Dynamics of Gothic Design*. Ashgate, 2011.  
[3] Erlande-Brandenburg, A. *The Cathedral Builders of the Middle Ages*. Thames & Hudson, 1995.
